Spatial surrogates of predictors

Source: R/surrogates.R
env_surrogates.Rd

Draws predictors with the same spatial autocorrelation as the observed ones but no relation to anything else, as null models for tests in landscapes with edges, where torus_permutations() do not apply or reject too often. They are the null options of pcps_test(), node_test() and phylo_beta_test(), which also take the list returned here (for example drawn with lonlat or strata), and also serve as null environments for simulations.

Usage

env_surrogates(
  env,
  coords,
  n = 99,
  method = c("variogram", "parametric"),
  lonlat = FALSE,
  strata = NULL
)

Arguments

env

Predictor, or matrix or data frame of predictors, with one row per site, such as an env_time matrix with one column per step. Or an mc_landscape, whose environment (or env_axes) is replaced, with the distances of the landscape.

coords

Matrix or data frame of coordinates with one row per site. Not needed for a landscape.

n

Number of surrogates, one whole number, 1 or more.

method

"variogram" or "parametric".

lonlat

Are coords longitude and latitude in decimal degrees (TRUE or FALSE)? Distances are then great-circle distances in kilometres.

strata

Optional group of each site, such as the city or the basin where it lies. Surrogates are drawn within each group on its own, so values never move between groups, which have their own autocorrelation. Each group needs at least 5 sites; a group where the predictors do not vary keeps them.

Value

List of n matrices with the dimensions and column names of env, or of n landscapes when env is one. For "parametric", attr(, "rows") is a matrix with one row per draw, giving for each site the row of env it received.

Details

"variogram" follows Viladomat et al. (2014): each predictor is permuted, smoothed with an exponential kernel over a proportion of its nearest sites, with the proportion chosen so that the variogram of the smoothed values best matches the observed one up to the 25% quantile of the distances between sites, and then rescaled, with independent noise for the nugget, so that the scale and intercept of the variogram match too. We use binned variograms rather than their kernel-smoothed one. With several predictors, all of them share the permutation of each draw, but each one gets its own smoothing, so their correlation is kept only approximately.

"parametric" fits an exponential range by maximum likelihood to the normal scores of the predictor, draws a Gaussian field with that range and gives the observed values to the sites in the order of the field, so each draw is a permutation of sites (in attr(, "rows")). With several predictors, the order is that of the first principal component of the scaled predictors, and whole rows move together, which keeps their correlation.

In data-raw/validation_continuous_nulls.R, for the site test of pcps_test() with one predictor and no relation, on a grid of 20 x 20 sites, an L-shaped region of 280 random points and a strip of 50 x 8 sites, with exponential ranges of 2, 5 and 10 sites, the rate of rejection at the 5% level was 0.025-0.09 (mean 0.062) for "variogram" and 0.03-0.10 (mean 0.066) for "parametric", against 0.24-0.79 for free permutations and 0.055-0.14 for the torus on the grid. Both became liberal (0.08-0.10) when the range approached the size of the landscape, when few independent patches of environment are left, so with broad fields p values near 0.05 deserve caution. These rates are for one predictor; with several, and in node_test() and phylo_beta_test(), they were not checked.

For simulations, env_surrogates() gives null environments: a landscape, or an env_time matrix, with the same spatial structure but no relation to the environment that shaped the observed communities. To ask whether a simulated pattern depends on where the environment is, rather than only on how much of it is autocorrelated, run the same simulation on the observed landscape and on its surrogates and compare a statistic. With env_time, "parametric" moves the whole series of each site to another site, so the dynamics of each site are kept and only their place changes; "variogram" smooths each step on its own, which does not keep the temporal autocorrelation. Landscapes keep their own distances, such as those of a torus, though the exponential covariance may then not be positive definite.

References

Viladomat, J., Mazumder, R., McInturff, A., McCauley, D. J., & Hastie, T. (2014). Assessing the significance of global and local correlations under spatial autocorrelation: a nonparametric approach. Biometrics, 70, 409–418. doi:10.1111/biom.12139

See also

torus_permutations(), rigid_permutations().

Other restricted null models: patch_permutations(), rigid_permutations(), torus_permutations()

Examples

set.seed(1)
coords <- as.matrix(expand.grid(1:12, 1:12))
field <- t(chol(exp(-as.matrix(dist(coords)) / 4))) %*% rnorm(144)
draws <- env_surrogates(field, coords, n = 3)
length(draws)
#> [1] 3
cor(field, draws[[1]])
#>           [,1]
#> [1,] 0.1758885
# null landscapes for the simulator
grid <- landscape_grid(10, env_range = c(0, 100))
nulls <- env_surrogates(grid, n = 2, method = "parametric")
cor(grid$env, nulls[[1]]$env)
#> [1] -0.2500471
